learningObjective: Compare CPU and GPU execution models on branch prediction, out-of-order execution, register file, and cache hierarchy design.

canonicalClaims.claim: CPUs are optimized for single-thread latency with large control-and-cache overheads (branch prediction, OoO issue, deep cache hierarchy) per core; GPUs are optimized for aggregate throughput with a large register file per SM and rely on massive TLP (many warps) for latency hiding, at the cost of higher per-op latency.
conditions: Modern data-center GPU (Ampere/Hopper) vs modern desktop/server CPU (Intel/AMD OoO).
nonImplications: Does not imply GPUs have no caches; L1 and L2 are present.
Does not imply CPUs cannot do SIMD; wide-vector ISAs are standard.

misconceptions.claim: GPUs do not use caches at all.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Modern GPUs have L1 (per SM) and L2 (per GPU) caches. Latency hiding via warp switching complements caches; it does not replace them.
misconceptions.sourceOrEvidence: CUDA C++ Programming Guide, memory hierarchy

misconceptions.claim: CPU cores have larger register files per core than a GPU SM.
misconceptions.whyWrong: A GPU SM's register file is on the order of 256 KB; a CPU core's architectural register file is a few KB (physical registers may be larger but still smaller than an SM's file).

misconceptions.claim: GPUs achieve throughput without any branch handling because SIMT is branch-free.
misconceptions.whyWrong: SIMT does handle branches, just with warp-level divergence serialization instead of speculative branch prediction.

implementationFacts: A100 SM: 65,536 × 4 B register file ≈ 256 KB per SM.
CPU cores (e.g., Zen4, Golden Cove) typically have ~32-48 KB L1D per core.
GPU latency hiding uses warp-level context switching, not branch speculation.
performanceScenarios: GEMM kernels benefit from GPUs' massive TLP and large register file; branchy irregular graph traversals often run better on CPUs.
